study.introduction: Researchers tested whether a night of sleep after learning helps people keep what they learned.
study.participants: 48 university students aged 18 to 22 in one US city, who reported no sleep problems. All gave informed consent and were paid.
study.method: At 9 p.m. every student studied 40 pairs of unrelated words (such as "river - candle") until they could recall at least 34. Students were randomly assigned to sleep normally in the lab (sleep group) or to stay awake all night under supervision (sleep-deprived group). Both groups then had a normal night of sleep the next night. Three days after learning, all students saw the first word of each pair and wrote the second.
study.results: The sleep group recalled an average of 31 of 40 pairs; the sleep-deprived group recalled an average of 24. A difference this large would be very unlikely if sleep made no difference.

plot.label: Bar graph of average word pairs recalled after three days: sleep group 31, sleep-deprived group 24, invented data

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether high school students who sleep more on school nights earn higher grades.
study.participants: 600 students in grades 9 to 12 at four public high schools in one US state. Parents gave permission and students agreed to take part.
study.method: Students wore a sleep tracker for four school weeks, giving their average sleep on school nights. Their end-of-term grade averages (on a 0 to 4 scale) came from school records with names removed.
study.results: Students who slept more had higher grades. Students who averaged under 6 hours had an average grade of 2.6; 6 to 8 hours, 3.0; more than 8 hours, 3.3. The correlation between hours of sleep and grades was $r = .32$.

plot.label: Bar graph of average grade by school-night sleep: under 6 hours 2.6, 6 to 8 hours 3.0, over 8 hours 3.3, invented data

sources.title: Short nights and learning new material

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether several short nights make it harder to take in new material the next day.
study.participants: 40 high school students aged 15 to 17 at a two-week summer program at a boarding school. Parents gave permission and each student agreed to take part.
study.method: Students were randomly assigned to 9 hours in bed or 5 hours in bed each night for five nights. Each afternoon they watched a 20-minute science lesson and then took a 20-question quiz on it. They also did a reaction-time task in which they pressed a key when a dot appeared; lapses were responses slower than half a second.
study.results: By the fifth day, the 9-hour group averaged 15 of 20 on the quiz and the 5-hour group 11 of 20. The 5-hour group had about three times as many attention lapses. Their quiz scores were lowest on the days they had the most lapses.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question.

rubric.point: States a defensible claim that answers whether sleep deprivation harms learning (for example, that losing sleep makes learning and remembering new information worse).
accept: losing sleep makes it harder to learn and remember new information
students who do not get enough sleep learn less

parts.sample: Sleep deprivation harms learning, because it weakens both taking in new information and holding on to it.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

rubric.point: Gives an accurate result (not a method or participant detail) from one source that supports the claim, and cites the source.
accept: In Source 1, students kept awake after learning recalled 24 of 40 pairs, compared with 31 for students who slept.
According to Source 3, the 5-hour group scored 11 of 20 on the quiz, compared with 15 for the 9-hour group.

parts.sample: In Source 1, students who stayed awake all night after studying recalled an average of 24 of 40 word pairs three days later, while students who slept recalled 31 (Source 1).

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim (the sleep-deprived group learned less, so missing sleep harmed learning).
accept: the group that missed sleep remembered fewer pairs, which shows learning was harmed

rubric.point: Applies a relevant psychology concept other than a restricted term, linked to the evidence (for example, consolidation theory: sleep after learning helps stabilize new memories).
accept: the hippocampus replays new learning during sleep

parts.sample: This supports my claim because the students who missed a night of sleep after studying kept fewer pairs, even though they slept normally the next night. Consolidation theory explains why: during the first night after learning, sleep helps stabilize new memories so they last. The awake group lost that night of consolidation, so less of what they studied was stored, which shows that losing sleep harms learning.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using a different piece of specific and relevant evidence from another source.

rubric.point: Gives an accurate result from a different source than in B(i) that supports the claim, and cites it.
accept: According to Source 3, after five short nights the 5-hour group scored 11 of 20 on the lesson quiz, compared with 15 for the 9-hour group.
In Source 2, students who slept under 6 hours had an average grade of 2.6, compared with 3.3 for those who slept over 8 hours.

parts.sample: According to Source 3, after five nights of only 5 hours in bed, students scored an average of 11 of 20 on a quiz about a new lesson, while students with 9 hours in bed scored 15 (Source 3).

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding than you used in B(ii).

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim (short sleep led to lower scores on learning new material).
accept: the short-sleep group learned less of the new lesson, which shows sleep loss harms learning

rubric.point: Applies a different relevant concept from B(ii), not a restricted term, linked to the evidence (for example, restoration theory, or the reticular activating system and alertness).
accept: restoration theory: without enough sleep the brain is not restored, so it works less well the next day
the reticular activating system controls alertness, and sleep loss led to attention lapses during the lesson

parts.sample: This supports my claim because the short-sleep students learned less from the same lesson. Restoration theory explains this: sleep lets the brain and body recover from the day's work, so a brain that has had five short nights is not restored and works less well. The 5-hour group had about three times as many attention lapses, and their quiz scores were lowest on their worst days, so an unrestored brain missed parts of the lesson. That shows sleep deprivation harms learning.
